name: Aisha Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Aisha, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Aisha, 27, single, and I still live at home with my mum and my younger sister, which is how I've saved so much. My brother Karim and I bought a small flat together two years ago and we rent it out, so that's my other bit of money. I left school at sixteen, did a hairdressing course I didn't finish, worked in a call centre, and I've been at the warehouse seven months. My family is big on working hard and not owing anyone anything.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a car parts distribution centre that supplies garages, so brake pads, filters, wiper blades, exhausts. Orders come in all day and the garages want them in two hours, so it's fast and noisy. I pick with a scanner and a trolley, and I'm honestly still slower than most because I mix up part numbers that look alike. I like the pace and learning what everything is. I use an AI app on my phone every day, mostly to plan my side project, which is a mobile tyre-fitting van, a van that goes to people's houses to change tyres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype? I'd be a bit surprised, I use it for loads already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool, not a miracle. I'd post something about how small businesses can still use it to save time. At work I'd say the old ways still work fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think great, it's a cheap helper for my van business and nobody big gets a huge advantage. My warehouse job stays, my rent from the flat keeps coming in. That's a good position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at the warehouse and save for the tyre van, which is about 15,000 for the van and the kit. I'd use AI to build the booking page and price the jobs. Then I'd start doing weekends with the van next spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually excited about the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where did the tyre-fitting idea come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the warehouse, honestly. I see how many tyres and parts go out to garages every day. My uncle used to have a garage, and he taught me one thing. People will always pay for someone to come to them, and that's what my tyre van is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interest rates, for the flat. If they go up, the mortgage on it eats the rent. That's real money worry, not robots.

say: I'd say AI is a **good tool**, not a miracle.
I'd post that **small businesses** can still use it to save time.
think: It's a **cheap helper** for my van business, with no big advantage for big firms.
My job stays and the **rent from the flat** keeps coming.
do: Save about **15,000** for the **tyre-fitting van** and kit.
Use **AI** to build the booking page and price jobs.
Start **weekend jobs** with the van next spring.
S0.quote: People will always pay for someone to come to them, and that's what my tyre van is for.
fieldNote: She sees AI as a **small-business helper**, consistent with free-market views.
A **rental flat** with her brother gives her a second income.
Her worry is **interest rates**, not technology.

steps.text: Save about 15,000 for a tyre-fitting van and kit
Build a booking page and price list using AI
Start weekend tyre jobs with the van next spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Booking, planning, answering customers. That's exactly what I want AI to do for the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for people who want to start something. I'd tell colleagues to learn the tools, not fear them. I'd post about my van, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's perfect timing. The admin side of a small business gets cheap, so one person can run it. My warehouse job might change a little, but robots are slow to arrive, so I'm fine while I build up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the van within the year and start weekends. I'd use AI to handle bookings, reminders and invoices. Once the van makes as much as the warehouse, I'd leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and pretty excited, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mum say about you leaving a steady job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd worry at first, then she'd brag about it to the aunties. My family respects people who build something. She'd just want me to keep the flat and not borrow too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would struggle in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people in our office who answer the garages' phones. That's exactly the kind of job AI takes. I'd tell them to think about what they could do with their hands.

say: I'd say it's **good news** for people who want to start something.
I'd tell colleagues to **learn the tools**, not fear them.
think: It's **perfect timing**, as cheap AI admin lets one person run a business.
Robots arrive **slowly**, so the warehouse job lasts while I build up.
do: Buy the **tyre van** within the year and start weekends.
Use **AI for bookings**, reminders and invoices.
Leave the warehouse once the van **earns as much**.
S1.quote: The admin side of a small business gets cheap, so one person can run it.
fieldNote: She sees thinking AI as a **business enabler**, not a threat.
Her family **respects building** something, which backs her plan.
She worries for **phone staff**, whose work AI takes first.

steps.text: Buy the tyre-fitting van within the year
Run bookings, reminders and invoices through AI
Leave the warehouse once the van matches her wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028 for AGI, then 2031 for robots that can do hands-on work. Okay, that's fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to shake everything up, but people who move fast will be okay. I'd say families need to back each other. I wouldn't call for handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my warehouse job goes by 2031. And the tyre van gives me a few more years, because changing a tyre on someone's drive in the rain is hard for a robot. But by the mid-2030s even that could go. So I'd need more than one income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the van straight away and work it hard for a few years to make money while I can. I'd keep the rental flat, since housing still matters when robots come. I'd put some money into the companies making the robots. And I'd use AI for everything that saves me time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not scared exactly, but I'd feel like I'm racing a clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the flat rather than put everything into the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people still need somewhere to live, whatever happens with robots. My brother and I bought it to have something solid. I wouldn't sell it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change any family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe wait on marriage a bit, if I'm honest. I'd want to know I can look after myself first. My mum wouldn't like that.

say: I'd say people who **move fast** will be okay.
I'd say **families** should back each other, not wait for **handouts**.
think: My **warehouse job** goes by 2031, when robots can pick.
The tyre van buys a few more years, but I'd need **more than one income**.
do: Buy the **van** straight away and work it hard.
Keep the **rental flat**, as people still need homes.
S2.quote: Changing a tyre on someone's drive in the rain is hard for a robot.
fieldNote: She uses the **three-year robot gap** to earn hard while hands-on work lasts.
She spreads risk across **business, property and shares**.
Even an adaptive person feels the **speed** here.

steps.text: Buy the tyre van straight away and work it hard
Keep the rental flat with Karim
Invest some savings in companies making robots
Delay marriage plans until her income is secure

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031, then 2034. That's a nice amount of time for a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's time to get ready, especially for anyone thinking of starting something. I'd post about my van. I'd tell my sister to learn AI now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I'm in a good place. Seven years of the van making money, plus the flat. I'd still lose the warehouse job, but I'd have left it by then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the van this year, then maybe a second van with someone working for me in three years. I'd use AI for the whole booking side. I'd keep saving and keep the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, because I can't see what happens after 2034. But mostly I'd be busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you hire someone, knowing robots are coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, for a few years. Someone gets a good job meanwhile, and I'd be honest with them about the timeline. That's better than no job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my little sister to learn the AI tools and a hands-on skill, both. One gets you started, the other keeps you working.

I'd tell my sister to **learn AI** now.
think: I'm in a **good place**: seven years of van income plus the flat.
I'd have **left the warehouse** before it's automated.
do: Buy the **van** this year and add a **second van** in three years.
Use **AI** for the whole booking side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, then 2039. That's a whole business lifetime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big opportunity for anyone willing to work. I'd tell young people to start something. I'd be pretty positive about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think I'm set. The van business, maybe two or three vans, the flat, and savings. I'd have years to figure out what's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the van this year, grow it, and use AI for all the admin. In five years I'd look at buying a second property with my brother. I'd keep working weekends myself to stay hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Really positive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could go wrong for you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If big companies bring in cheap robot tyre vans and undercut me, I'd sell the business while it's still worth something. I'd see that coming a few years out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from government in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly stay out of the way and keep taxes low for small businesses. Maybe help with training for people who need it, but not handouts.

I'd tell young people to **start something**.
think: I'm **set**: the van business, maybe two or three vans, the flat and savings.
I'd have **years** to figure out what's next.

fieldNote: Ten years turns her plan into a **growing business**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's barely time to build the business before the robots arrive. What would help is low taxes for small businesses and cheap loans to buy kit like vans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about building things. Everyone asks what you'd lose, but some of us are thinking about what we could start.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks what you'd lose, but some of us are thinking about what we could start.
portrait: Aisha is a **27-year-old picker** at a car parts warehouse, living with her mum and sister.
She co-owns a **rental flat** with her brother and uses AI daily.
She plans a **mobile tyre-fitting van** and sees thinking AI as cheap admin help.
Fast AGI makes her **anxious**; more time turns her plan into a growing business.
She wants **low taxes** and cheap loans, not handouts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving too little time to build the business.
whatWouldHelp: **Low taxes** for small businesses and **cheap loans** for kit.
